article_title: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD)
citation: Self-Regulated Strategy Development: WWC Intervention Report. (2017). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.thinksrsd.com
title: Teach self-regulation skills alongside academic strategies so students can apply strategies without guidance
description: SRSD pairs explicit instruction in a concrete academic strategy with instruction in self-regulation skills, so that students come to apply the strategy independently. The report states: "A key part of the process is teaching self-regulation skills, such as goal-setting and self-monitoring, which aim to help students apply the strategy without guidance." Teachers instruct students in monitoring and evaluating their strategy use, model both the strategy and self-regulation, and gradually transfer responsibility until students perform tasks without support.
requirements: Teachers provide support tailored to student needs, frequent constructive feedback, and positive reinforcement during the supported-practice stage.
constraints: The intervention begins with teacher direction and ends with students independently applying the strategy; effectiveness evidence in this report covers students with specific learning disabilities in grades 2 through 10.
target_learners: Students with learning disabilities in grades 2 through 12
target_learning_goals: Independent application of academic strategies such as essay planning and organizing ideas before writing
examples: In the model-the-strategy stage, teachers use a think-aloud process and voice positive self-statements; students set individual targets to improve on baseline performance.
key_sources: Self-Regulated Strategy Development: WWC Intervention Report. (2017). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/680

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: Self-Regulated Learning theory as a lens for DLP trace data
description: The paper presents SRL theory as one of three frameworks connected to DLP data. SRL concerns how students actively plan, monitor, and evaluate their learning, and DLPs allow detailed tracking of these behaviors through time-on-task data, hint usage, and problem-solving attempt sequences. The authors note studies citing ASSISTments log data on planning prompts and self-assessment, showing 'SRL scaffolds support not only learning outcomes but also offer researchers a window into students' metacognitive decision-making in real time.'
requirements: DLP environments must log behaviors traceable to SRL phases, such as time-on-task, hint requests, and sequence of problem-solving attempts
constraints: The authors state the examples are illustrative, 'not to validate any of these frameworks as dominant in the field,' and more often theories are applied post hoc rather than built into platform design
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners using digital platforms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning behaviors: planning, monitoring, help-seeking, and reflection
examples: The paper cites ASSISTments studies of planning prompts, reflective questions, and self-assessment mechanisms (Inventado et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020)

citation: Shan Zhang, Ruiwei Xiao, Anthony F. Botelho, Guanze Liao, Thomas K. F. Chiu, John Stamper, and Kenneth R. Koedinger. 2026. How to Assess AI Literacy: Misalignment Between Self-Reported and Objective-Based Measures. In LAK26: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026). title: Paired self-report and objective-based AI literacy assessment instruments for K–12 teachers
description: The study developed two psychometrically validated instruments aligned to Ng et al.'s four AI literacy dimensions: a 25-item scenario-based objective MCQ test and a 15-item (refined to 13) five-point Likert self-report scale adapted from AILS-CCS. Items were "written in a scenario-based format that situates test-takers in realistic pedagogical contexts and requires them to engage with AI to solve educational problems". Both were validated with 288 Taiwanese K–12 teachers and function as diagnostic tools for professional development.
requirements: Items aligned to an established AI literacy framework shared across both measures
Translation and piloting with a local teacher to check wording and cultural nuances

Some existing technical items in related instruments may capture unfamiliarity with technical terminology rather than the capacity to integrate AI into practice

examples: Data were collected in February 2025 from over 2,000 Taiwanese teachers via mailing lists; 358 completed the survey and the final analytic sample was 288

The article posits a reciprocal relationship in which CT offers structured problem-solving approaches supporting SRL, while SRL supports metacognitive control in computational problems.

constraints: The framework was applied to eighth-grade students in a four-week Python coding context with a specific AICA tool

citation: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8
title: Systematic reviews as intentional learning experiences scaffolded by mentoring that combines methodological guidance with emotional scaffolding
description: The article frames systematic reviews "as intentional learning experiences that unfold across stages of the review and require mentoring and technological support." Mentoring is described as "an integrated support system that combined methodological guidance with emotional scaffolding" rather than solely procedural knowledge transmission. Mentoring was embedded across stages: guiding search refinement, joint discussion of borderline screening decisions, and collaborative coding, reducing the cognitive and emotional burden of evaluative judgments and supporting both technical competence and confidence.
requirements: Mentoring support embedded across multiple stages of the review process, or peer-based discussion groups when individual mentoring is not feasible
constraints: The account draws on one team's experience conducting an SR in the interdisciplinary LDT field; the authors position it as a practical guide for similarly complex fields

examples: Experienced researchers guided novices in refining search scopes and selecting databases; mentoring at screening involved joint discussion of inclusion and exclusion decisions for borderline cases

article_title: SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging
citation: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982
title: SRJudge: a three-stage Select-Reason-Judge framework for fine-grained knowledge concept tagging
description: SRJudge decomposes knowledge concept tagging into three stages. A fine-tuned BERT-based Selector first narrows the candidate space: "the Selector first picks K(≪ |Φ|)candidates ... reducing the decision space". A lightweight LLM Reasoner, trained with a pruned GRPO reinforcement-learning strategy and a task-specific reward combining format, accuracy and dynamic position rewards, recommends a concept with reasons over the shortlist. A frozen larger LLM Judger then evaluates the rationality of the reasoning and issues the final verdict from a global perspective. The framework addresses the problem that LLMs "struggle to select the correct concept from a large-scale candidate set due to the high dimensionality of the decision space".
requirements: A labeled dataset for supervised fine-tuning of the Selector, plus unlabeled instances for continued pre-training, as the article states the Selector is fine-tuned on a labeled dataset
constraints: The Reasoner operates only on the top-K shortlist produced by the Selector, so concepts outside the shortlist cannot be selected
target_learners: educational platforms and MOOCs tagging exercises for grade 7-12 mathematics, biology and physics
target_learning_goals: accurate assignment of fine-grained knowledge concept labels to exercises and solutions
examples: On S Math, S Bio and S Phy, the Selector shortlists K=5 candidates, the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct Reasoner reasons over them under GRPO, and Qwen3-32B acts as Judger
key_sources: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982

article_title: The Relationship Between AI Anxiety and Academic Motivation Among University Students: The Mediating Role of Emotion Regulation and the Moderating Role of Gender
citation: Zhang Y, Shi Y and Lu J (2026). The relationship between AI anxiety and academic motivation among university students: the mediating role of emotion regulation and the moderating role of gender. Front. Psychol. 17:1918525. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1918525
title: Moderated mediation model linking AI anxiety to academic motivation through emotion regulation, with gender as a boundary condition
description: The article proposes a moderated mediation model, grounded in self-regulated learning theory, in which AI anxiety — 'a situation-specific emotional response' to generative AI use — is linked to academic motivation through emotion regulation, with gender moderating the second stage. It conceptualises AI anxiety as 'a contextual demand rather than treating AI solely as a learning resource', and emotion regulation as a personal resource that helps students maintain goal orientation under AI-related uncertainty.
requirements: Requires measures of AI anxiety, emotion regulation and academic motivation; the study used a four-item AI anxiety scale adapted from UTAUT technology anxiety, the 10-item Emotion Regulation Questionnaire, and a 20-item Academic Motivation Scale
constraints: The model was tested with cross-sectional self-report data, which the article states 'does not permit causal conclusions or establish the temporal ordering' of the variables
The article notes the findings 'extend and refine rather than revise the core propositions of SRL theory' given the cross-sectional design
target_learners: university students in AI-supported learning contexts
examples: The study tested the model with PROCESS Models 4 and 14 on responses from 1,484 Chinese university students, using 5,000 bootstrap resamples and bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals

citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Self-regulated learning as a multi-component construct with metacognitive, cognitive, and resource management strategies
description: The article treats self-regulated learning as a multi-component construct whose trainable components include SRL knowledge, metacognitive strategies, cognitive strategies, and resource management strategies. It reports that participants "improved on SRL knowledge, metacognitive strategies, cognitive strategies (elaboration, organisation and critical thinking), and resources management strategies (time-management and effort regulation)". The training program's structure mirrors this taxonomy, with dedicated content on learning strategies, resource management, and metacognitive strategies, and the three phases of SRL.

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: SRI program: sustained multiple-strategy instruction grounded in self-regulated learning and cognitive apprenticeship
description: The SRI program aims "to create independent self-regulated readers who are capable of applying appropriate reading strategies in various contexts." It draws on self-regulated learning theory and cognitive apprenticeship, teaching a limited set of nine strategies (predicting, relating to background knowledge, monitoring, deriving word meaning from context, visualizing, questioning, generating main idea, summarizing, evaluating) before, during, and after reading. Teacher modeling occurs in the meaningful context of reading aloud award-nominated children's literature three times weekly, followed by independent reading of self-chosen books with a strategy checklist on which students note problems and solutions, and weekly transfer lessons in content areas such as science. Regulation gradually shifts from teacher to students across the two years.
requirements: Teachers receive training (two three-hour meetings, a mid-year meeting, and an evaluation meeting) with video clips demonstrating strategy modeling, plus observation and coaching in November of each year
A collection of narrative and informative books at varied levels must be available for independent reading
constraints: Experimental schools were not allowed to use their own reading comprehension curriculum for the duration of the study
target_learners: Third and fourth grade elementary students of varying reading levels
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and self-regulated use of reading strategies
examples: In Grade 3 strategies were introduced one by one over nine weeks; in Grade 4 three strategies were modeled at a time and students increasingly assisted in modeling
key_sources: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: Read-aloud lesson structure integrating modeling, independent reading, and reflection
description: Each SRI lesson follows a fixed 40-minute structure: "(a) introduction of 5 minutes, (b) 15 minutes reading aloud including 5 minutes modeling of one or two strategies to the whole class, (c) 15 minutes individual independent reading with application of strategies and making notes, and (d) 5 minutes whole-class evaluation." The pattern embeds strategy modeling in authentic, motivating read-alouds of children's literature, then has students immediately apply the modeled strategies during independent reading of self-chosen books, recording problems and solutions on a strategy checklist, and closes with whole-class reflection on whether the strategy helped comprehension.
requirements: Well-written, interesting children's literature with manuals highlighting two or three moments to model a strategy
A strategy checklist and folder for each student
constraints: Teachers initially reported difficulty fitting the lessons in forty minutes, though they became accustomed to the structure during the year
target_learning_goals: Application of reading strategies during authentic reading
examples: Books included works by Tosca Menten, Mirjam Oldenhave, and Lydia Rood; students chose books from classroom or school libraries at their own reading level

Educational Research Review, 28, 100292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2019.100292
title: SRL as a three-phase process comprising metacognitive and resource management activities
description: The article adopts an SRL framework in which self-regulating learners are "metacognitively, behaviorally, and motivationally active" and proceed through a preparatory, performance, and appraisal phase. Metacognitive activities include goal setting, strategic planning, comprehension monitoring, strategy regulation, and reflection; behavioral and motivational regulation (time management, environmental structuring, help seeking, effort regulation) are grouped as resource management activities. The framework structures how interventions and measures are coded in the meta-analyses.
requirements: Learners must possess an adequate repertoire of cognitive strategies to be able to successfully self-regulate, per the article's rationale for the cognitive-strategies moderator.
constraints: Task motivation (task value, goal orientation, self-efficacy) is treated as a precursor outside SRL, following the models the article adheres to.
examples: The coding scheme classified SRL measures and intervention targets into metacognitive and resource management activity categories clustered for the moderator analyses.

title: Three-relations mediation framework linking SRL interventions, SRL activity, and achievement
description: The article organizes the field around three relations: the effect of SRL interventions on achievement (relation 1), the effect of interventions on SRL activity (relation 2), and the relation between SRL activity and achievement (relation 3), with SRL activity hypothesized as the mediator. Prior reviews each covered only part of this framework; this study is presented as the first comprehensive meta-analysis including all three relations at once, enabling a formal mediation test via MASEM.
requirements: Estimating the mediation requires data on all three relations; the article notes only three primary studies included statistical information on all three.
constraints: MASEM could not yet apply three-level models for nested effect sizes or evaluate continuous moderators, per the article's stated shortcomings.

examples: The framework (Fig. 1) guided the literature searches, coding scheme, and the three research questions about factors influencing each relation.

article_title: Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback
citation: Steinert, S., Avila, K. E., Ruzika, S., Kuhn, J., & Küchemann, S. (2024). Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00354-1
title: Self-regulated learning as interplay of cognition, metacognition, and motivation, supported by formative feedback
description: The article's theoretical background frames self-regulated learning as a mental activity in which individuals control thoughts, actions, and feelings to steer their learning, built on three key processes: cognition (acquiring knowledge and understanding), metacognition ("thinking about thinking", i.e., planning, monitoring, and adjusting strategies), and motivation (the readiness to exert effort toward goals). Formative feedback delivered during learning is presented as a crucial component for supporting these SRL strategies by stimulating metacognitive processes such as self-monitoring. LEAP is designed to address all three dimensions through different prompt types.
requirements: Feedback must be specifically related to the task or learning process, providing information on current performance and guidance on closing the gap to the targeted comprehension
constraints: Adaptive learning support can be counterproductive if it merely reiterates existing knowledge, leading to an expertise reversal effect
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational processes
examples: The article's six scaffold types map onto the three SRL dimensions: cognitive (sense-making, elaboration, self-explanation, partial task solution), metacognitive, and motivational

article_title: Self-regulated learning training programs enhance university students’ academic performance, self-regulated learning strategies, and motivation: A meta-analysis
citation: Theobald, M. (2021). Self-Regulated Learning Training Programs Enhance University Students' Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, and Motivation: A Meta-Analysis. Contemporary Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cedpsych.2021.101976
title: SRL strategy taxonomy: cognitive, metacognitive, and resource management strategies within a three-phase cyclical process
description: The article organizes self-regulated learning as a dynamic, cyclical process in which "learning sessions can be divided into three phases: a preparatory phase, a performance phase, and an appraisal phase." Learners' strategies are classified into three families: cognitive strategies (rehearsal, elaboration, organization) that acquire and integrate knowledge; metacognitive strategies (goal setting and planning, monitoring, reflection) that monitor and control cognition across all phases; and resource management strategies regulating internal resources (attention, effort, motivation) and external resources (learning environment, time management). The article uses this taxonomy to categorize training outcomes in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Training programs must address the specific SRL strategy families (cognitive, metacognitive, resource management) that the taxonomy distinguishes for their effects to be classified and compared.

title: Self-regulated learning as a cyclical process model with cognitive, motivational, affective and metacognitive components
description: Self-regulated learning is a central construct of pedagogical psychology in which a learning session is conceptualized as a cycle: objectives and planning, implementation and monitoring, and final evaluation of results. Existing models share cognitive, motivational, affective and metacognitive components. The article cites Zimmerman's triadic interaction, Winne and Hadwin's four phases, and Boekaerts' three areas, and notes these models are being applied to online and mobile learning environments.
requirements: Metacognitive control of the learning process is described as an essential prerequisite for self-regulated learning
examples: The article describes models applied to new educational contexts including online and mobile learning environments using digital technologies

article_title: The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving
citation: Soederberg Miller, L. M., & West, R. L. (2010). The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving. Experimental Aging Research, 36(1), 40-63. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610730903418380
title: Self-Regulation of Language Processing (SRLP) model: readers regulate attention based on goals and perceptions of goal progress via internal and external feedback loops
description: The Self-Regulation of Language Processing model holds that as individuals strive to comprehend a text, they regulate their attention based on their goals and perceptions of how well they believe they are meeting those goals. Readers compare actual comprehension to desired comprehension and use this information, through internal feedback loops and external sources of performance information, to adjust attention. The article states that "individuals compare their actual comprehension levels to their desired comprehension levels and use this information to adjust their attention to meet these goals." This study tested the model's prediction that external feedback influences self-regulatory responses during reading.
requirements: Feedback information, whether intrinsic or extrinsic, must be interpretable by the reader as indicating progress toward or away from reading goals

citation: Nugteren, M. L., Jarodzka, H., Kester, L., & Van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2018). Self-regulation of secondary school students: self-assessments are inaccurate and insufficiently used for learning-task selection. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9448-2

description: The self-regulated learning-task selection (SRLTS) model describes "a systematic way in which students could select tasks to develop their knowledge and skills". Adapted from Zimmerman's SRL cycle and Van Merriënboer and Kirschner's dynamic task-selection model, it has students self-assess via performance estimates, mental effort ratings, and JOLs, compare these to internal standards, and use the gaps to choose a next task's difficulty, support, and content. title: SRL-AIDE: a professional development model combining direct and indirect SRL instruction through authentic, interactive, dynamic live-actor simulation experiences
description: SRL-AIDE (Authentic, Interactive, and Dynamic Experiences in SRL context) is a teacher professional development model combining explicit instruction in SRL theory and practice with simulations in which professional actors play student roles and one participant teaches. The article states it "involves live-actor simulations, where participants are highly engaged and immersed in the experience." After each simulation, participants analyze scenarios with metacognitive prompts, receive feedback from audience and actors, and take part in a guided video-based debriefing. title: Newly developed SRL strategy knowledge test with 25 paired strategy comparisons
description: A newly developed strategy knowledge test presents an academic learning scenario (preparing an oral presentation in educational psychology) divided into forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, where participants rate the usefulness of strategy pairs on a four-point scale. Scoring uses "the relative judgment of superiority respective of inferiority of strategies" across 25 paired comparisons, with a maximum sum score of 50. Reliabilities were 0.71 (metacognition), 0.76 (motivation), and 0.84 (cognition).
requirements: Categorization into useful and not useful strategies based on theoretical assumptions and expert evaluations; an explicit hint that the task rates general usefulness, not one's own practice

examples: In the study, the strategy knowledge test was administered first, before the learning task, and its cognition scale correlated −0.33 with GPA

title: The SRL&T approach: an integrated framework of self-regulated learning and teaching
description: The SRL&T approach is the article's conceptual framework for understanding how teachers facilitate development of their own and their students' SRL by transitioning between roles. The article states it "provides a conceptual framework for understanding how teachers can facilitate the development of their own and their students' SRL by transitioning between different roles", enabling feedback aligned with three teacher perspectives: as self-regulated learners, as teachers, and as mentors. title: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD): explicit, staged strategy instruction for writing self-regulation
description: SRSD is an intervention that explicitly teaches students writing strategies and the self-regulation skills to deploy them independently, with the long-term goal that students implement strategies in new contexts without teacher prompting. Strategies are taught through staged instruction in which the teacher "first presents the strategies to students, then models their use, proposes exercises to consolidate these strategies in memory, and supports students in their first implementation until they can perform these tasks autonomously". Students also learn a self-evaluation strategy of checking whether the important parts of a narrative text were included. The planning sheet offers a series of subgoals and supports retrieving ideas from long-term memory.

title: Self-regulation factor framework predicting learning strategy use: eagerness, vigilance, MCSR, self-control, attention control, effort regulation, and engagement
description: The article draws on a review of influential SRL models (Panadero, 2017) to propose a set of self-regulation factors that might predict individual differences in students' use of learning strategies. It states: "our overview of pivotal SRL models enabled us to propose a set of self-regulation factors (eagerness, vigilance, MCSR, self- control, attention control, effort regulation, and engagement) that might predict individual differences in students' use of learning strategies". Each factor is grounded in a major SRL model: goal-related processes appear in all major models, MCSR in Zimmerman's, Efklides', Pintrich's and Winne and Hadwin's models, and effort regulation in Efklides' and Pintrich's models. Engagement is added as a factor not explicitly considered in leading SRL models but overlapping with many aspects of SRL.

constraints: The article states the set of predictors is not exhaustive: "we do not propose an exhaustive set of predictors"

citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

description: The SRM model addresses the reciprocal relationship between value and interest when students self-regulate. The article states it "integrates motivation to reach goals (predicted by value and expectancy of reaching the goals) and motivation based on the subjective experience of interest while working towards those goals." When interest ebbs, individuals consider whether there is a sufficient reason to continue; if so, they may either continue as is or engage in strategies to enhance the experience of interest, potentially changing how they perform the activity.

citation: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4
title: Time management within SRL comprises forethought, performance-phase monitoring, and control strategic processes
description: The review frames time management as a self-regulatory process within SRL, defined as students' strategic efforts to plan, monitor, and regulate when and for how long they engage in academic work. Core processes include goal setting, prioritizing, planning, and time estimation in the forethought phase; monitoring of time passage in the performance phase; and control processes that adjust time allocation. The article states that "Effective goal setting, prioritization, and planning all rely on students' anticipations... of how long it will take to finish academic work." Procrastination is treated as antithetical to time management and indicative of a failure in SRL.
requirements: Students must form expectations about the duration of academic work, though the article notes estimation "can be challenging and fraught with errors"
constraints: No well-established canon of fundamental time management tactics exists, and no widespread standard conceptual definition has been established

target_learning_goals: effective self-regulated management of academic study time

description: The article proposes a conceptual framework that unifies four SR research traditions—Stable Dispositions, Limited Resources, Driving Forces, and Learning Activities—into one architecture. It states: "our framework positions SR as a dynamic, interdependent system, emphasizing how interactions and compensatory mechanisms explain individual differences and influence learning outcomes." target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of cognition, motivation, emotion, and behavior in pursuit of learning goals

description: Using a Lakatosian framework of research programs, the article categorizes SR research into four traditions, each with a hard core of foundational assertions protected by a belt of auxiliary hypotheses and methods. The article states: "we categorize existing research programs into four broad traditions, each of which is characterized by its core explanatory construct family: (1) Stable Dispositions, (2) Limited Resources, (3) Driving Forces, and (4) Learning Activities." constraints: The traditions were selected because they present distinct assumptions, mechanisms, and constructs of individual-level SR; contextual factors are excluded from the taxonomy

target_learning_goals: Understanding how dispositions, cognitive resources, motivation, and learning strategies each explain self-regulation
examples: The Learning Activities tradition's hard core centers on metacognitive monitoring and control of learning activities (Winne & Hadwin), while the Limited Resources tradition foregrounds working-memory capacity and executive functions

title: Hierarchical model of nested self-regulatory cycles at macro, meso, and micro levels
description: Drawing on action regulation theory, the framework proposes that self-regulatory processes occur across nested cycles at three levels of granularity and timescale. The article states: "These cycles can be conceptually segmented into three distinct levels: the macro-level (e.g., managing long-term goals such as preparing for an examination across multiple study sessions or an entire semester), the meso-level (e.g., executing within-session cycles of planning, performance, and appraisal), and the micro-level (e.g., adjusting strategies in response to real-time feedback or moment-to-moment monitoring)."

constraints: The segmentation is conceptual, proposed by the authors drawing from action regulation theory rather than empirically tested in this article

target_learning_goals: Coordinating long-term goal pursuit, within-session regulation, and real-time strategy adjustment
examples: A poor micro-level self-test result may trigger motivational regulation inflected by trait conscientiousness, leading to deeper strategies in future meso-level sessions

title: Instructional elements of learning environments that foster SRL indirectly: complex activities, choices, and evaluation criteria
description: The article identifies instructional elements of learning environments relevant for students' engagement in SRL, including "offering complex and meaningful activities" and "providing choices about the content, the place, or the cooperation partner while working on an assignment", choices about the level of challenge, and providing evaluation criteria. These elements, drawn from Perry's research, have proven to distinguish between classrooms that support students in enacting SRL and those that do not. Related preconditions include self-direction, cooperative learning, constructivist learning principles, and fostering transfer.

constraints: Complex learning environments with much information but minimal structure or guidance will be detrimental for learning since they increase cognitive load; constructivist environments are more effective when they provide explicit guidance

citation: Romain Quentin, Lison Fanuel, Mariann Kiss, Marine Vernet, Teodóra Vékony, Karolina Janacsek, Leonardo G. Cohen and Dezso Nemeth. (2021). Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period. npj Science of Learning 6:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00093-9
title: SRT and ASRT task designs distinguishing general skill, statistical, and high-order rule learning
description: The serial reaction time (SRT) task presents a deterministic 12-element sequence; the alternating serial reaction time (ASRT) task interleaves four predetermined elements with four random ones, creating an eight-element probabilistic sequence. Trial types (pattern, random-high, random-low) allow the article to state that the structure "allows the distinction between (i) general skill learning, measured by a decrease in RT for all trials, (ii) statistical learning, measured by the difference in RT between the random-high trials and the random-low trials ... and (iii) high-order deterministic learning, measured by the difference in RT between pattern trials and random-high trials."
requirements: Blocks binned into five bins to compute online and offline gains; warm-up trials, repetition and trill triplets, and error trials discarded from analyses
constraints: In the SRT task with only deterministic transitions, general skill cannot be dissociated from sequence learning within each block or rest period; high-order rule learning was only observable in the long ASRT task

target_learning_goals: implicit visuomotor sequence learning and its subcomponents
examples: Experiment 1 used the SRT task with 63 participants in two sessions 12 h apart; Experiments 2 and 3 used the ASRT task with 180 and 25 participants respectively

title: Four-code scheme for coding self-initiated SRL processes by type (cognitive vs. metacognitive) and accuracy (high vs. low)
description: For sequence mining, the authors coded every self-initiated SRL behavior from log files into "separate codes (see Table 1) of behaviors, which contained two separate elements, with four codes in total (2 × 2)": cognitive-high accuracy, cognitive-low accuracy, metacognitive-high accuracy, metacognitive-low accuracy. constraints: Only self-initiated processes were coded, so externally prompted behaviors from pedagogical agents were excluded
target_learners: college students learning with an intelligent tutoring system
target_learning_goals: measuring sequences of cognitive and metacognitive self-regulated learning processes
examples: Notes were compared to content pages with Latent Semantic Analysis, with scores of 50% similarity and higher coded as accurate.

title: Genre-teaching routine combining memorable experiences with SRSD elements including the IPEELL mnemonic
description: This instructional pattern pairs memorable experiences (such as trips to local landmarks or visits from World War II veterans) with a fixed set of SRSD teaching elements used whenever a specific genre is taught. title: Self-regulation based reading lesson plans structured in forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases with gradual responsibility transfer
description: The article's intervention program organized Turkish course lesson plans in three phases: "The lesson plans were organized in three phases that are; "Forethought Phase", "Performance Phase," and "Self -Reflection" phase in alignment with self -regulating strategies". title: SDL-R interpreted through Zimmerman's SRL phases and Grow's Staged Self-Directed Learning Model
description: The article interprets self-directed learning readiness through two complementary frameworks: Zimmerman's cyclical self-regulated learning model (forethought, performance, self-reflection) and Grow's Staged Self-Directed Learning Model, in which learners "progress from dependent to self-directed participants through iterative stages of autonomy". The four SDLI domains are mapped onto SRL phases: learning motivation to forethought, planning and implementation to forethought-performance, self-monitoring to performance-reflection, and interpersonal communication as cross-phase socially mediated regulation. requirements: SDL-R is measured via the validated 20-item SDLI whose four domains are conceptually aligned with SRL phases for interpretation
constraints: SDL and SRL are distinct constructs: SDL emphasizes autonomous control of the learning process, whereas SRL describes internal cognitive and motivational mechanisms; the frameworks are complementary, not interchangeable
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning readiness, self-regulated learning, lifelong learning capacity
examples: The study used the frameworks to guide subgroup analyses: semester variation tests sensitivity to curricular timing consistent with Grow's staged model, and the M1 Spring decline followed by M2 recovery is read as progression toward autonomous self-direction

article_title: Role of self-regulated learning in a communication skills curriculum: a mixed-methods study.
citation: Delibalta B, Güner Y, Üçüncüoğlu M, Türk Y, Dilbaz AD, Ateş E, Aykut DS. (2026). Role of self-regulated learning in a communication skills curriculum: a mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09417-y
title: SRL-based communication curriculum combining microlearning preparation, simulation, SP feedback, and debriefing
description: A first-year communication skills curriculum pattern structured around three steps per simulation session: "(1) preparation with the materials, (2) attending the simulation and receiving feedback from simulated patients, and (3) debriefing." Microlearning materials (short videos, documents of no more than two pages, audio-embedded presentations) were shared via the education management system in advance, positioning preparation as the student's SRL responsibility, while SP feedback and subsequent debriefing supported reflection. The curriculum was designed vertically across six years using Kern's six-step approach, with a curriculum map shared with educators and students.
requirements: Students are expected to study shared materials in advance and arrive prepared for simulation; educators direct students to adequate resources as scaffolding.
constraints: Implemented only with first-year medical students; the program should be continued and evaluated in upper years as a vertical curriculum.
The study did not examine the differential impact of individual curriculum components.
target_learning_goals: communication skills and positive communication attitudes
examples: Basic pain scenarios (headache, shoulder pain, knee pain) were used in simulations; SPs provided feedback based on a basic communication skills guide after each simulation.

title: Self-regulated learning as a framework for curriculum design, with microlearning as scaffolding
description: The article applies self-regulated learning — "taking responsibility for individuals' own learning by setting goals, planning, monitoring, and evaluating" — as the theoretical foundation for curriculum design. Within this framework, microlearning-based materials function as scaffolding: diversified short materials shared in advance support preparation, engagement, and reflection, while educators direct students to adequate resources and provide opportunities for self-evaluation. The authors interpret their findings within SRL as "a multidimensional and interconnected process rather than a set of isolated strategies," citing evidence that strategies such as note-taking, environmental structuring, self-evaluation, and self-consequences function as an integrated system with self-evaluation playing a central role.
requirements: Students need a target to achieve and must know what they should learn, especially in early medical education; educators must scaffold by directing students to adequate resources and guiding self-evaluation.
constraints: A lack of self-evaluation can lead to a lack of learning; monitoring and self-evaluation are described as the most complex SRL steps for medical students.
examples: The study operationalised SRL scaffolding as microlearning-based materials embedded in the educational management system, with preparation linked to positive emotions and increased motivation.

description: The organizing framework of the intervention: self-regulated learning as a cyclical, dynamic process in which students regulate cognitive, affective-motivational and behavioural aspects to reach personal goals. The model posits three interconnected phases: "In the planning phase, students construct a representation of the task, engaging in planning strategies and goal setting"; a monitoring phase in which students tackle the task while regulating performance; and an evaluating phase of self-evaluation and regulation. article_title: Psychological skills and their educational outcomes in adolescence: self-regulation, time management, and academic self-efficacy.
citation: Çobanoğlu Necati, Gökalp Serkan. (2026). Psychological skills and their educational outcomes in adolescence: self-regulation, time management, and academic self-efficacy. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04368-x
title: Integrated account positioning self-regulation as foundational capacity, time management as behavioral mechanism, and academic self-efficacy as cognitive outcome
description: The article integrates Bandura's self-efficacy theory with Zimmerman's cyclical model of self-regulated learning, in which learning proceeds through "forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases". Within this integration, "the current study positions self-regulation as a foundational psychological capacity, time management as the behavioral mechanism through which this capacity is enacted, and academic self-efficacy as the resulting cognitive outcome". Time management is treated as a behavioral pathway translating regulatory capacity into efficacy beliefs via mastery experiences. The SEM findings are offered as empirical support for this integrated model.
requirements: Measurement of all three constructs within a single structural model using validated scales
constraints: Grounded in cross-sectional self-report data from a single Turkish university, so temporal ordering is not established
examples: The study tested the framework with 450 undergraduates using the ASRI, the Time Management Skills Scale, and the Academic Self-Efficacy Scale in a latent-variable SEM

title: Williamson Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning (SRSSDL)
description: The SRSSDL, developed by Williamson in 2007, is a 60-item self-report instrument with a five-point Likert scale (1–5) used in this study to measure nursing students' self-directed learning ability. Its five dimensions are awareness, learning strategies, learning activities, evaluation, and interpersonal skills, with 12 items each; scores range from 60 to 300, and a score above 200 indicates a high level of self-directed learning. constraints: Self-report basis; the study's limitations note self-reports may not accurately reflect actual levels of self-directed learning and clinical competence
target_learners: third- and fourth-year undergraduate nursing students
examples: Used with 450 nursing students in western Iran, yielding a mean total score of 240.04 ± 32.14

title: Set of translated and adapted instruments (SRIS, SRQ-L-PJ, PCS, CS) for assessing self-reflection, regulation, and competence in German final-year medical students
description: A battery of German-translated and adapted questionnaires developed per the Artino et al. framework: the 20-item SRIS measuring self-reflection and insight, the SRQ-L-PJ for autonomous and controlled regulation, a 12-item perceived competence scale (PCS), and a 10-item competence scale (CS) based on NKLM 2.0 entrustable professional activities. title: SRSSDL: Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning (60-item, five-area instrument)

article_title: Assessment IS learning: developing a student-centred approach for assessment in Higher Education.
citation: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921
title: Self-regulated learning comprises cognitive, metacognitive and motivational/affective domains, each with behaviours and mental processes
description: The article situates student-centred assessment within self-regulated learning (SRL). It states that 'Models of self‐regulated learning that focus on cognitive strategies, typically highlight three domains (summarised in Fig. 1): cognitive, metacognitive and motivational/affective'. The cognitive domain covers how learners process, retain and retrieve knowledge and skills; the metacognitive domain audits and regulates the cognitive domain; the motivational/affective domain concerns motivations, rationales, intended outcomes and goals. The article adds, citing Lehmann et al., that each domain consists of two components—behaviours/actions and mental processes—each needing mastery by the learner.
requirements: For assessment to be effective as an instrument for learning it needs to support the development of SRL; guidance is required to transform external measurements of performance into internalised personalised standards
constraints: SRL is primarily a personal process, but interactions with others and the local environment, including co-regulation and socially shared regulation, also matter
target_learners: higher education students developing independence as learners
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of cognitive strategies, behaviours, motivations and environments
examples: The review argues assessment can provide avenues for co-regulated and socially shared regulation, and that explicit modelling of self-assessment strategies should be embedded within the learning process

title: Self- vs. Externally-Regulated Learning (SRL vs. ERL) theory
description: The SRL vs. ERL theory frames self-regulation (SR) as a presage variable, a general meta-ability to manage decisions by planning, exercising control and evaluating effects, which "facilitates self-regulated learning (SRL), as process, in the academic achievement". It also assigns the context an external-regulatory/non-regulatory/dys-regulatory role, so both personal regulation and family socio-educational level are modeled as predictors of achievement, self-efficacy and procrastination. This study operationalizes the theory by predicting adolescent achievement from SR, self-efficacy, procrastination and parents' educational level.

examples: The study clustered students into low/medium/high self-regulation and family socio-educational groups and tested their effects on achievement with ANOVA/MANOVA

citation: Bennion Layne D., Durning Steven J., LaRochelle Jeffrey, Yoon Michelle, Schreiber-Gregory Deanna, Reamy Brian V., Torre Dario. (2018). Untying the Gordian knot: remediation problems in medical schools that need remediation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1219-x
title: Self-Regulated Learning—Microanalytic Assessment and Training (SRL-MAT) as a three-phase cyclical remediation approach
description: SRL-MAT is a problem-solving approach to remediation, adapted by Durning and associates from a self-directed learning process that is generic to topic and context. It functions as a three-phase cyclical loop applicable across learning situations: "(a) Forethought including strategic planning and motivational factors, (b) Performance involving metacognitive monitoring, self-testing and self-control and (c) Self-Reflection about performance such as causal attribution, self-evaluation and satisfaction". The paper notes it rests on educational research showing successful learning outcomes across multiple contexts and has been used to improve medical students' diagnostic reasoning.
requirements: Requires application of the three cyclical phases (forethought, performance, self-reflection) to immediate and longer-term work products
constraints: The paper presents it as an alternative to matching remediation strategies to specific student deficits rather than as a validated individualization procedure
examples: The paper describes the model as successfully utilized in improving the diagnostic reasoning of medical students

citation: Sagasser MH, Kramer AWM, Fluit CRMG, van Weel C, van der Vleuten CPM. (2016). Self-entrustment: how trainees' self-regulated learning supports participation in the workplace. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-016-9723-4
title: Socio-cultural framing: trainees' SRL enacts legitimate peripheral participation, moving them from periphery toward the centre of the workplace community
description: The article interprets its findings through socio-cultural learning theory, specifically Lave and Wenger's legitimate peripheral participation. It argues that "By performing SRL in clinical workplaces learners might influence their participation in practice and their sense of legitimacy", and that exercising SRL activities "bolstered trainees' self-entrustment and their self-perceived growth in competence, and it increased trainees' legitimacy and promoted their move to the centre". Agency and interaction with supervisors are central to this process.
requirements: A practice that affords trainees space to act independently, supervisor trust, clear access to supervisors, and access to information sources.
constraints: Legitimacy is partial: trainees felt able to act independently while also "feeling assured not to have all competencies yet".
target_learners: Novice postgraduate trainees entering workplace communities of practice
target_learning_goals: Professional identity development and increasing legitimate participation in clinical practice
examples: Trainees expressed legitimacy as being able to act independently and being part of the practice.
